interest: This file provides extraordinary insight into the bureaucratic and ideological origins of the occupation's 'reverse course,' showcasing intense inter-agency clashes between the State Department and the Army over abandoning hardline trust-busting (FEC 230) in favor of economic reconstruction. Historians will particularly value primary materials such as the complete 31-page James L. Kauffman report attacking SCAP policies, records of direct conversations with Japanese officials like Shigeto Tsuru, Holding Company Liquidation Commission corporate designation rosters, and diplomatic documentation of Chinese and Soviet opposition to Japan's industrial resurgence.
keywords: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (SCAP)
overview: This file documents United States inter-agency and occupation economic policy toward post-World War II Japan between September 1945 and early 1948, chronicling the critical transition from initial punitive demilitarization, zaibatsu dissolution, and reparations removals toward industrial rehabilitation and self-support. Through diplomatic despatches, SWNCC/SANACC policy papers, SCAP reports, and correspondence, the records illuminate the bitter debates between the State Department and the Department of the Army over multilateral cooperation through the Far Eastern Commission versus unilateral economic directives. The collection also details Japan's severe domestic economic distress—including runaway inflation, food shortages, and wage-price controls under the Katayama Cabinet—alongside operational programs such as the Occupied Japan Export-Import Revolving Fund, trade revival initiatives, and the implementation of the Deconcentration Law (Law No. 207).
